items.prompt: What is the 'same-origin policy'?
choices: The browser's default rule that JavaScript on one origin can't read responses from a different origin, unless that origin opts in
A rule requiring all API servers to be hosted on the same physical machine as the frontend
A DNS setting that prevents two websites from sharing a domain name
A convention where all requests must use HTTPS
items.explanation: The same-origin policy is specifically about JavaScript being restricted from reading cross-origin responses by default — it's a browser-enforced rule, not a hosting or DNS requirement.
items.reference:
Same-origin policy
🌐 Own origin: always allowed
🚫 Other origin: blocked by default
Why: CORS is the mechanism that lets a server opt back into cross-origin access.

items.prompt: According to L1, does the same-origin policy apply to tools like Postman and curl?
choices: No — it's a browser-enforced rule, which is why the same request works in Postman but not in the browser
Yes — Postman and curl enforce the exact same restrictions as browsers
It depends on which operating system Postman is running on
L1 doesn't address whether other tools enforce it
items.explanation: L1 is explicit that this is a browser-side restriction — Postman and curl simply don't enforce it, which is exactly why the same request succeeds in one and fails in the other.
items.reference:
Same-origin policy
🌐 Own origin: always allowed
🚫 Other origin: blocked by default
Why: CORS is the mechanism that lets a server opt back into cross-origin access.

items.prompt: What is CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing)?
choices: The mechanism a server uses to opt in to cross-origin requests, via specific response headers the browser checks
A protocol for encrypting traffic between two different servers
A caching layer that speeds up cross-origin requests
A JavaScript library that must be installed to make any API call
items.explanation: CORS is specifically the opt-in mechanism, expressed through response headers — not an encryption protocol, caching layer, or required library.
items.reference:
CORS
🔓 Server opts in via headers
👀 Browser checks before handing data over
Why: it's what lets a server override the same-origin default.

items.prompt: According to L1, who enforces the CORS check — the server or the browser?
choices: The browser — the server can process and respond normally regardless of CORS
The server — it refuses to process requests from disallowed origins
Both enforce it equally, at different stages
Neither — CORS is enforced by a separate proxy layer
items.explanation: L1 states this directly — CORS enforcement happens on the browser side, after the server has already processed the request and sent a response.
items.reference:
CORS
🔓 Server opts in via headers
👀 Browser checks before handing data over
Why: it's what lets a server override the same-origin default.

items.prompt: What is a 'preflight request'?
choices: An automatic OPTIONS request the browser sends before certain cross-origin requests, asking the server if it would allow the real one
The very first request a browser ever sends when a page loads
A request sent by the server to verify the client's identity
A manual test request a developer sends before deploying code
items.explanation: A preflight is specifically an automatic OPTIONS check the browser sends before certain requests — not a page-load event or a manual developer action.
items.reference:
Preflight request
❓ OPTIONS: "would you allow this?"
➡️ Real request only sent if approved
Why: it lets the browser check before committing to a potentially risky cross-origin action.

items.prompt: According to L1, what does the Access-Control-Allow-Origin header do?
choices: It tells the browser which origins are allowed to read the server's responses
It tells the server which origins are allowed to send requests to it
It encrypts the response body for the specified origin only
It sets a timeout for how long a request can take
items.explanation: The Access-Control-Allow-Origin header is a response header the server sends telling the browser which origins may read that response — not a request filter or encryption mechanism.
items.reference:
Preflight request
❓ OPTIONS: "would you allow this?"
➡️ Real request only sent if approved
Why: it lets the browser check before committing to a potentially risky cross-origin action.

items.prompt: According to L2's table, is a GET request with a custom Authorization header a 'simple' request?
choices: No — the Authorization header alone makes it non-simple, even though GET itself is a simple method
Yes — GET is always simple regardless of headers
It depends on the value of the Authorization header
Only DELETE and PUT can ever be non-simple
items.explanation: L2's table specifies that only a narrow set of headers count as simple — Authorization isn't among them, so it triggers preflight even with a simple method like GET.
items.reference:
Simple vs. non-simple
Method: GET/HEAD/POST only
Headers: a narrow allowed list
Why: a single non-simple header is enough to require a preflight.

items.prompt: According to L2's table, does a POST request with Content-Type: application/json count as simple?
choices: No — application/json isn't in the simple Content-Type list, so it triggers a preflight
Yes — POST is always simple regardless of Content-Type
Yes, as long as the request body is small
L2's table doesn't address Content-Type at all
items.explanation: L2's table lists only a few specific Content-Type values as simple — application/json isn't one of them, so it triggers a preflight.
items.reference:
Simple vs. non-simple
Method: GET/HEAD/POST only
Headers: a narrow allowed list
Why: a single non-simple header is enough to require a preflight.

items.prompt: According to L2's sequence diagram, what happens if the preflight response doesn't include the calling origin?
choices: The browser stops there — the real request is never even sent
The browser sends the real request anyway, just without credentials
The server automatically retries with a different origin
The preflight is simply skipped and the real request proceeds normally
items.explanation: L2 states plainly that a failed preflight stops the browser before the real request is sent at all — nothing about the real request proceeding regardless.
items.reference:
The preflight sequence
OPTIONS → check → real request (if approved)
Why: a failed preflight means the real request is never sent at all.

items.prompt: According to L2, what does a simple (no-preflight) request's browser-side check look like compared to a non-simple one?
choices: The request is still sent and processed by the server, but the browser checks Access-Control-Allow-Origin on the actual response instead of a preflight
Simple requests skip all CORS checks entirely and always succeed
Simple requests are checked before sending, exactly like non-simple ones
L2 doesn't distinguish between simple and non-simple request handling
items.explanation: L2 explains that simple requests skip only the preflight step — the browser still checks the actual response's Access-Control-Allow-Origin before releasing it to JavaScript.
items.reference:
The preflight sequence
OPTIONS → check → real request (if approved)
Why: a failed preflight means the real request is never sent at all.

items.prompt: According to L2's table, does fetch()'s promise reject on a 500 Internal Server Error response?
choices: No — it resolves normally, with response.ok set to false
Yes — any 4xx or 5xx status always causes fetch() to reject
It depends on whether the browser is Chrome or Firefox
It rejects only if the 500 response has no body
items.explanation: L2's table is explicit: HTTP error statuses like 500 resolve fetch()'s promise normally, with response.ok reflecting the failure — they don't cause a rejection.
items.reference:
Does fetch() reject?
Network / CORS failure → rejects
404 / 500 response → resolves, ok: false
Why: try/catch alone doesn't catch HTTP error statuses.

items.prompt: According to L2, is a CORS block distinguishable from a plain network failure just by looking at whether fetch()'s promise rejected?
choices: No — L2 states they're indistinguishable that way, both simply reject
Yes — CORS blocks throw a distinctly different error type
Yes — CORS blocks always include the blocked origin in the error message
L2 doesn't address whether these two cases can be told apart
items.explanation: L2's table notes CORS blocks and network failures both cause fetch() to reject, and are indistinguishable from a promise-rejection perspective alone.
items.reference:
Does fetch() reject?
Network / CORS failure → rejects
404 / 500 response → resolves, ok: false
Why: try/catch alone doesn't catch HTTP error statuses.

items.prompt: According to L3's verified needsPreflight results, does a plain GET with no headers need a preflight?
choices: No — needsPreflight('GET', {}) returns false
Yes — every GET request needs a preflight regardless of headers
Only if the response body is larger than 1KB
L3 doesn't test this specific case
items.explanation: L3 verifies needsPreflight('GET', {}) returns false — a plain GET with no custom headers is a simple request.
items.reference:
needsPreflight, verified
GET, {} → false
GET, {Authorization} → true
Why: a single non-simple header flips the whole request to non-simple.

items.prompt: According to L3, does adding an Authorization header to a GET request change whether it needs a preflight?

It depends on the specific value of the Authorization header, not just its presence
items.explanation: L3 verifies this exact flip — adding Authorization makes needsPreflight return true, confirming headers alone can force a preflight regardless of method.
items.reference:
needsPreflight, verified
GET, {} → false
GET, {Authorization} → true
Why: a single non-simple header flips the whole request to non-simple.

items.prompt: Implement `simulateFetchResolution(status, networkFailure)`: a synchronous stand-in for what `fetch()` resolves or throws for, matching L3's `mockFetch` logic. If `networkFailure` is true, throw `new TypeError('Failed to fetch')`. Otherwise, return `{ ok: status >= 200 && status < 300, status }` — note that a 404 or 500 does NOT throw here, it just returns `ok: false`.

tests.description: a 404 does not throw — it returns ok: false
tests.expr: (() => { return expect(simulateFetchResolution(404, false)).toEqual({ ok: false, status: 404 }); })()
(() => { return expect(simulateFetchResolution(200, false)).toEqual({ ok: true, status: 200 }); })()

tests.description: a genuine network failure throws TypeError('Failed to fetch')
tests.expr: (() => { let threw = false; let msg = ''; try { simulateFetchResolution(0, true); } catch (e) { threw = true; msg = e.message; } return expect(threw && msg === 'Failed to fetch').toBeTruthy(); })()

items.explanation: This mirrors exactly what L3's mockFetch does — an HTTP error status like 404 doesn't throw, it just comes back with ok: false, while only a genuine network-level failure throws. This is the core reason a bare try/catch around fetch() misses HTTP errors entirely.
items.reference:
The fetch() gap, verified
404 response → success: true (buggy)
404 response → success: false (fixed)
Why: checking response.ok is the only way to catch an HTTP error status.

items.prompt: Implement `checkResponseOk(response)`, matching L3's `getUserFixed` logic: given a `{ ok, status }` object, throw `new Error('Request failed with status ' + response.status)` if `response.ok` is false. Otherwise, return `response.status`.

tests.description: returns the status for a successful response
throws with the exact message for a 404
tests.expr: (() => { let threw = false; let msg = ''; try { checkResponseOk({ ok: false, status: 404 }); } catch (e) { threw = true; msg = e.message; } return expect(threw && msg === 'Request failed with status 404').toBeTruthy(); })()

tests.description: throws with the exact message for a 500
tests.expr: (() => { let threw = false; let msg = ''; try { checkResponseOk({ ok: false, status: 500 }); } catch (e) { threw = true; msg = e.message; } return expect(threw && msg === 'Request failed with status 500').toBeTruthy(); })()

items.explanation: This is the explicit check L3's getUserFixed adds on top of a plain await fetch(...) — turning an HTTP error status into a thrown error is what routes it into the same catch block already handling network failures, giving one consistent error-handling path for both.
items.reference:

404 response → success: true (buggy)
404 response → success: false (fixed)
Why: checking response.ok is the only way to catch an HTTP error status.
